Alice has a cake, and she is going to cut it. She will perform the following operation n−1n-1n−1 times: choose a piece of the cake (initially, the cake is all one piece) with weight w≥2w\ge 2w≥2 and cut it into two smaller pieces of weight ⌊w2⌋\lfloor\frac{w}{2}\rfloor⌊2w​⌋ and ⌈w2⌉\lceil\frac{w}{2}\rceil⌈2w​⌉ (⌊x⌋\lfloor x \rfloor⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉\lceil x \rceil⌈x⌉ denote floor and ceiling functions, respectively).

After cutting the cake in nnn pieces, she will line up these nnn pieces on a table in an arbitrary order. Let aia_iai​ be the weight of the iii-th piece in the line.

You are given the array aaa. Determine whether there exists an initial weight and sequence of operations which results in aaa.

Input

The first line contains a single integer ttt (1≤t≤1041 \le t \le 10^41≤t≤104) — the number of test cases.

The first line of each test case contains a single integer nnn (1≤n≤2⋅1051 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^51≤n≤2⋅105).

The second line of each test case contains nnn integers a1,a2,…,ana_1, a_2, \ldots, a_na1​,a2​,…,an​ (1≤ai≤1091 \le a_i \le 10^91≤ai​≤109).

It is guaranteed that the sum of nnn for all test cases does not exceed 2⋅1052 \cdot 10^52⋅105.

Output

For each test case, print a single line: print YES if the array aaa could have resulted from Alice's operations, otherwise print NO.

You may print each letter in any case (for example, YES, Yes, yes, yEs will all be recognized as positive answer).

Note

In the first test case, it's possible to get the array aaa by performing 000 operations on a cake with weight 327327327.

In the second test case, it's not possible to get the array aaa.

In the third test case, it's possible to get the array aaa by performing 111 operation on a cake with weight 1 970 429 4731\,970\,429\,4731970429473:

  • Cut it in half, so that the weights are [985 214 736,985 214 737][985\,214\,736, 985\,214\,737][985214736,985214737].
Note that the starting weight can be greater than 10910^9109.

In the fourth test case, it's possible to get the array aaa by performing 222 operations on a cake with weight 666:

  • Cut it in half, so that the weights are [3,3][3,3][3,3].
  • Cut one of the two pieces with weight 333, so that the new weights are [1,2,3][1, 2, 3][1,2,3] which is equivalent to [2,3,1][2, 3, 1][2,3,1] up to reordering.
